snippet.title: The Deadliest Mercenaries - Genoese Crossbowmen DOCUMENTARY
snippet.description:
History documentary on the Genoese Crossbowmen! Check out this Crusade inspired book from our community "A Remedy for Mercy" https://www.amazon.com/Remedy-Mercy-Myles-Kearsley/dp/B0FWYPXPGJ/ref=tmm_pap_swatch_0

We continue our series on the most famous Units of History with a deep dive on the Genoese Crossbowmen. This begins with the historical origins of both the crossbow and the city state of Genoa. We then see how these two came together to form the first of the Genoese Crossbowmen. We then trace their development over the Medieval era across the Crusades, the 100 Years War, the Renaissance, and more. Along the way we cover their equipment, training, and organization as a military unit.

snippet.title: The Roman Disaster Worse Than Cannae — The Battle of Arausio (105 BC)
snippet.description:
Forget everything you think you know about Roman defeats. While Cannae is famous, an earlier battle was far more devastating, nearly ending the Roman Republic a century before Caesar. This is the story of the Battle of Arausio.

In 105 BC, on the banks of the Rhône River, two massive Roman armies converged to face a terrifying migration of Germanic tribes: the Cimbri and the Teutones. What followed was a perfect storm of arrogance, rivalry, and military disaster. The result? A loss so staggering it’s considered the single worst military defeat in Roman history by the number of lives lost.

In this video, we dive into:
🔍 The clash of cultures: The Roman legions vs. the nomadic Germanic warriors.
⚔️ The fatal flaw: How toxic rivalry between Roman consuls doomed their armies.
💀 The scale of the horror: Why the casualty numbers at Arausio dwarf those of Cannae.
🏛️ The political shockwave: How this disaster triggered the Marian Reforms and set the stage for the fall of the Republic.
🛡️ The man who saved Rome: Gaius Marius and his rise to power in the aftermath.

This isn't just ancient history; it’s a lesson in hubris, survival, and military transformation. How did Rome recover from its greatest defeat? And why was Arausio almost erased from popular memory?

snippet.title: The Battle of Leuthen (1757): Frederick the Great’s Masterpiece
snippet.description:
Artwork from the channel collected into a coloring book (line art + colored versions):
https://amzn.to/4veRAb4
It also includes some illustrations that haven’t appeared in the videos yet.
(Disclosure: As an Amazon Associate we earn from qualifying purchases.)


It is December 5, 1757. Frederick the Great, king of the rising Prussian state, rides through the clear, icy winter air. Upon reaching a small hill near the village of Leuthen, he looks out on an overwhelming sight. As far as the eye can see, the enemy line stretches across the horizon. Sixty-six thousand Austrian soldiers—nearly twice the number he commands—stand ready to face his exhausted troops. At Leuthen, the Prussians set an enduring example of how linear tactics were best executed. The battle is widely regarded as one of the greatest—perhaps the greatest—military achievements in Europe during the Ancien Régime. Even Napoleon praised it as “a masterpiece of movements, maneuvers, and resolution.”  This is how modern historiography recounts the story of the Battle of Leuthen.

snippet.title: The Viking Trap That Slaughtered an English Army — Battle of Edington (878)
snippet.description:
August 10, 991. The black tide of Viking longships surges up the Blackwater River, heading for the shores of Essex. 🚣‍♂️💀 On the banks, a seasoned English commander named Byrhtnoth watches with grim determination. He has the advantage—the causeway connecting Northey Island to the mainland is narrow, defensible, and completely under his control. But then, pride, overconfidence, or perhaps sheer chivalry moves him to do the unthinkable. He lets the Vikings cross. And an English army marches to its slaughter. This is the Battle of Maldon—the day a noble gesture became a national tragedy. ⚔️🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿💔

In this video, we wade into the blood-soaked waters of the Blackwater estuary to witness one of the most haunting episodes in Anglo-Saxon history. Discover how one fateful decision—an act of hubris immortalized in one of England's greatest poems—destroyed an army, paved the way for Danegeld, and sealed England's fate under Viking domination.

snippet.title: The Secret Weapon That Broke the Ottoman Navy — Lepanto (1571)
snippet.description:

snippet.title: He Traveled From Norway to Guard the Byzantine Emperor.
snippet.description:
Sometime in the 11th century, a Norse warrior standing guard inside the Hagia Sophia pulled out his knife and carved his name into the marble parapet of the upper gallery. The inscription reads: Halvdan was here. It is still visible today.
Halvdan was a member of the Varangian Guard — elite Norse mercenaries who served as the personal bodyguards of the Byzantine emperor from 988 AD onward. To join, a recruit paid an entry fee of sixteen pounds of gold. Monthly salary was forty nomismata. When an emperor died, the Guard was permitted to enter the Imperial palace and take whatever they could carry. Loyalty had a price. Byzantium paid it precisely.
In battle they wore blue tunics beneath crimson cloaks, Byzantine lamellar armor, and carried gilded axes taller than a man. They traveled from Scandinavia through Russia's river systems — navigating cataracts, fighting off ambushes — before reaching Constantinople. The journey alone killed the weak.
Sweden eventually passed a law forbidding men from inheriting property while serving in Constantinople. The empire was draining Scandinavia of its finest warriors and not returning them.
Halvdan didn't carve a prayer or a battle cry. Just his name. In the marble of the greatest cathedral in the world.

snippet.title: It Survived 1,500 Years. The Last Stones Built a Fortress.
snippet.description:
The word for lighthouse in French is phare. In Italian, faro. In Spanish, faro. In Romanian, far. Every one of those words descends from the same source — a building that hasn't existed for over 600 years.
The Pharos of Alexandria was completed around 280 BC on a small island in Alexandria's harbor. It took 33 years to build, cost twice the Parthenon, stood over 110 meters tall, and burned a continuous fire visible 40 kilometers out to sea. At its peak it was one of the tallest man-made structures on earth. Ancient sources claimed its bronze mirrors could set enemy ships alight from across the Mediterranean. Almost certainly myth — but the fact that people believed it tells you everything about what this building meant.
Three earthquakes — 956, 1165, and 1303 AD — dismantled it over centuries. The traveler Ibn Battuta visited in 1326 and found it partially ruined. He returned in 1349. The entrance had collapsed completely. By 1480 the last of its stones were recycled into a medieval fortress built on the same spot.
That fortress still stands. The lighthouse is gone — except in the language of millions who have never heard of it.

snippet.title: How Peasants Trapped and Slaughtered 30,000 Knights — The Ambush That Saved Wallachia
snippet.description:
The Biggest Ambush in Europe — Posada 1330. An army of 30,000 Hungarians enters a narrow mountain pass… and discovers there is no escape. For days, the cliffs rain down boulders, arrows, and chaos, turning the road into a death trap as wagons jam, formations collapse, and panic spreads through the column.

In this episode, we break down how the Wallachian voivode Basarab I set the trap, why the Hungarian campaign unraveled, and how the terrain itself became a weapon. Step by step, you’ll see the strategy, the mistakes, and the brutal mechanics of an ambush designed to destroy an army from above.

snippet.description:
Take the battle to the Warhammer 40.000 universe and play Tacticus for free: https://play.tacticusgame.com/SandRhomanHistoryOct

Siege warfare in Japan differed fundamentally from that in Europe. While European sieges were revolutionized at the end of the Middle Ages by the emergence of artillery and bastion forts, guns and siege engines played only a minor role in Japan. Instead, Japanese armies often favored direct assault tactics to capture fortresses. Japanese castles were also designed with a different defensive approach in mind. Rather than relying on a massive outer wall to stop the enemy, as in Europe, Japanese defenses were based on the principle of defense in depth. Attackers were forced to navigate a carefully engineered labyrinth of death, where defenders launched counterattacks, ambushes, and rained down stones, arrows, and bullets. The second half of the 16th century witnessed numerous spectacular sieges, during which fortresses were burned, undermined, or even deliberately flooded. In this video, we explore how to lay siege to a Japanese castle during the Sengoku period.

snippet.description:
In 1565, just 600 Knights of St John and a few thousand Maltese defenders faced the Ottoman Empire’s 40,000 men in the Great Siege of Malta.
Outnumbered more than sixty to one, they held the line, saving Europe from invasion and changing history forever.
This cinematic historical documentary tells the story of faith, courage, and strategy that stopped an empire and defined Europe’s last great stand.
